title: Let the Qudit Do the Jacobi: A Structured Quantum Algorithm for Spectral Decomposition
abstract: Jacobi diagonalization is a long-established numerical algorithm for the spectral decomposition of Hermitian and, more generally, normal matrices. In this work, we develop a qudit-native quantum realization of the Jacobi diagonalization algorithm for unknown unitary operators. The proposed framework avoids explicit reconstruction of the operator and controlled-unitary operations. Each elementary two-parameter Givens rotation is implemented through two sequential single-parameter quantum variational optimizations that are directly accessible experimentally. An interferometric protocol is further introduced for extracting the eigenvalues of the diagonalized unitary, up to an overall global phase. Numerical simulations on ensembles of Haar-random unitary matrices demonstrate that the proposed algorithm preserves the characteristic convergence behavior of the classical Jacobi method and exhibits the expected quadratic scaling in the number of elementary operations with the dimension $d$, comparable to its classical counterpart. The results establish the proposed algorithm as a structured quantum numerical linear algebra algorithm naturally suited to qudit architectures and provide a bridge between classical iterative matrix algorithms and their quantum realizations.
summary: This paper presents the Jacobi Qudit Algorithm (JQA) for finding the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of unknown unitary operators acting on qudits. It achieves this by mapping the iterative Givens rotation steps into sequential, experimentally accessible single-parameter variational optimizations. The work is significant because it establishes a structured quantum method that mirrors classical numerical efficiency while being naturally suited for qudit architectures.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a quantum algorithm for spectral decomposition of unknown unitary operators, specifically realizing the Jacobi diagonalization procedure on qudits.
main_result: The proposed structured quantum algorithm preserves the convergence behavior of classical Jacobi methods and achieves expected quadratic scaling ($O(d^2)$) in elementary operations with dimension $d$.
method: It implements Givens rotations using two sequential, experimentally accessible single-parameter quantum variational optimizations rather than explicit operator reconstruction or controlled unitaries.
model_or_system: The system is a qudit (dimension $d$) undergoing unitary evolution governed by an unknown unitary operator. The method mimics the classical Jacobi algorithm for normal matrices.
key_observables: Convergence of the off-diagonal norm ($	au(M)$), eigenvalues extracted via interferometry, and the number of required Jacobi sweeps.
important_parameters: The dimension $d$ of the qudit space; the target accuracy $\epsilon$; and the structure of the unitary operator $M$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that elementary two-parameter Givens rotations can be decomposed into two sequential single-parameter variational optimizations, which are experimentally feasible.
figures_summary: Figure 3 compares the average number of Jacobi sweeps required for different accuracies ($\epsilon$) across dimensions $d$, showing the scaling behavior of the JQA compared to generic methods.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem by relating it to classical Jacobi diagonalization, details the qudit-native quantum realization using sequential variational optimizations for Givens rotations, discusses eigenvalue extraction via interferometry, and concludes with complexity analysis and future directions like parallelization.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete blueprint for implementing complex numerical linear algebra routines directly on hardware (qudits), offering a structured path from classical theory to quantum circuit realization.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Overview of the proposed Jacobi Qudit Algorithm (JQA). (a) Iteration scheme for a single Jacobi step acting on the (p, q) subspace. Each iteration consists of two successive one-dimensional quantum variational searches (QVS), determining the optimal parameters of the real and imaginary Givens rotations, followed by the corresponding updates of the transformed operator. (b) Quantum variational search used to determine each rotation parameter. The local cost function is evaluated through repeated measurements of the observable B on the computational basis states |p⟩and |q⟩, and the optimal rotation angle ˜ϕ is obtained by minimizing the resulting one-dimensional cost landscape. FIG. 2: Evolution of the average off-diagonal cost function log(τ(M)) as a function of the pivot count for d = 20, averaged over fifteen Haar-random unitary matrices. The solid curve represents the ensemble average, while the error bars indicate one standard deviation. The double vertical marks (||) denote the completion of successive Jacobi sweeps. The nearly linear decrease during the first sweeps, followed by a progressively faster decay, is characteristic of cyclic Jacobi-type diagonalization algorithms.
